title: Can Alpine bounce back and take the P5 fight to Racing Bulls?
excerpt:
The battle between Racing Bulls and Alpine for fifth place in the World Championship has been one of the subplots of the 2026 season, and at the moment it’s advantage to the Italian team.

A strong run through the Azerbaijan, Bahrain and Singapore triple header saw Racing Bulls log 23 points, while Alpine scored none. It’s left the former with a handy advantage of 32 points with six rounds to go, including this weekend’s United States Grand Prix at COTA.

That’s a decent lead, but it’s not done yet, given that Alpine famously scored 33 points in a single soggy afternoon when Esteban Ocon and Pierre Gasly finished second and third at Interlagos in 2024.

The big frustration for the Enstone team is that the A526 has been competitive at every track, and often faster in Qualifying than the VCARB 03, but that hasn’t been translated into results – most infamously in Azerbaijan, where Franco Colapinto and Gasly collided.

In contrast, Racing Bulls have generally capitalised on their opportunities, notwithstanding the contact between Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson in the same event.

“There's been quite a few races we haven't really been as quick as them, but we've outscored them,” says the New Zealander. “Baku we got lucky, the team got lucky. And I feel like that outside of that, we've actually just done a really good job.”

Alpine’s challenge is to bounce back from the recent difficult run and score consistently over the remaining races.

“It's clear that we lost the last triple header, and we need to win this one,” says Colapinto. “We need a kind of stop, a reset, and a start from zero again. And it's tricky in F1 when everything comes very fast, and you have one weekend to another to another, and then you are in the sim.

“We were a long time in the factory four days after the race in Singapore, trying to find some performance for the future and trying to understand the issues we've got.

“I think in general again it's not to overanalyse anything, we don't need to go super into detail of every little bit, but generally it's been a couple of tough weekends.

“We mostly understand why. We also were not the luckiest, but you can clearly see it. So again, we'll need a bit of luck this last part of the year, but I'm sure we can do a good end of the season.”

It’s been a trend that the car has been more competitive over one lap than in race trim – related to tyre usage – although Colapinto suggests that the difference in form is perhaps not as marked as you might think.

“I feel like we've been competitive in general on Saturdays for sure,” he says. “On Sundays we've been strong as well. For the most part of the year, we were up there, and the races have been fighting for points. We look super strong.

“It's true that for me, Malaysia is tricky to say because of the weather, and the roughness of the track I think was something very specific. But then, in general Baku, Madrid, the hot races, we were in this very hot European season, and we were strong on Sundays. So I don't think it's something to be super concerned [about].

“I think we are normally stronger on Saturday than Sundays. That's a reality. But it's not that we are slow on Sundays. We are good, and we are looking to extract more pace of the car.”

Gasly says that the team isn’t doing anything fundamentally wrong, and the run of non-scores over the last triple header was just a sequence of unfortunate events.

“I think looking at Qualifying, we qualified in the Q3s in all three races, four including the Sprints,” says the Frenchman. “So the pace in quali has been good. In the race it was mixed bag of unlucky events – looking at the Baku race, in Sepang that was kind of like 50:50 with the starting tyre, and we got it wrong unfortunately, and Singapore, which I think unfortunately highlighted the main limitation of the car that we have in a race at the moment.

“So it was just all compacted in these three weeks, and obviously we've been very disappointed, because we had we lost a lot of ground to VCARB, and we expected quite a lot more points at the end of it.”

Gasly insists that P5 isn’t lost – and he’s hoping that history repeats.

“I think personally, I just want to take it race-by-race,” he says. “It's a big gap. At the same time, with that team I've seen back in 2024 we've had that amazing double podium in Brazil, and all of a sudden we had plenty of points scored.

“So it's never impossible. It's a tough challenge, but I think we've just got to take one race at a time, trying to do the best job we can. And then we'll do the maths at the end of the year.”

title: Crawford set for Mexico City FP1 outing with Aston Martin
excerpt:
Jak Crawford will take the wheel of Lance Stroll’s AMR26 during FP1 at the Mexico City Grand Prix, marking his fourth on-track appearance of the 2026 season.

Acting as Aston Martin’s Third Driver, Crawford drove in Free Practice sessions in Japan, Austria and Belgium and achieved a highest finish of P20 at the Red Bull Ring.

His upcoming FP1 running, announced during his home race weekend at the United States Grand Prix, will fulfil the team’s mandated rookie practice sessions for the year.

Since concluding his third campaign in Formula 2 last year, the 21-year-old has completed crucial testing and simulator work for the team as they sought to improve their underperforming power unit and chassis.

“I'm really looking forward to getting back behind the wheel of the AMR26 in Mexico City,” said Crawford, who joined the Aston Martin Driver Development Programme in 2024.

“It's a special circuit for me as it's where I made my FP1 debut last year, so it's great to return with more experience under my belt.

“I've learned a lot through my time on track and in the simulator this season, and I'm looking forward to putting that into practice.

“It's also special to be announcing this during my home race weekend in Austin. As always, the focus will be on making the most of the session and delivering useful feedback for the team.”

Chief Trackside Officer Mike Krack added: “We are pleased to give Jak another opportunity in the AMR26. He returns to Mexico City with considerably more experience than when he made his FP1 debut there last year.

“His contributions through our simulator and testing programmes have been valuable, and this session provides another opportunity to demonstrate his capabilities while supporting the team's preparations for the weekend.”

title: McLaren drivers 'still allowed to race' each other – Norris
excerpt:
Lando Norris has offered an update on McLaren's intra-team orders ahead of the United States Grand Prix, after the reigning World Champion and team mate Oscar Piastri collided at the previous round in Singapore.

Norris and Piastri collided on the final lap of the Sprint, with Norris ultimately accepting responsibility for the incident despite the stewards deciding it was a racing incident.

Speaking on Thursday's media day in Austin, Norris revealed that both he and Piastri would be able to race each other, but that any repeat collision would not be tolerated.

"I got plenty of telling-offs, and plenty of words have been said. But we’re still allowed to race," said Norris.

"But of course, we can’t have what happened last weekend, or what happened here last year [where the pair collided at Turn 1 in the Sprint], happening again.

"So, no, we’re still allowed to race, but obviously we can’t have a coming together, and we have to avoid that at every opportunity possible."

McLaren have failed to match their form from the summer, where Norris claimed two victories in Hungary and the Netherlands, as well as three pole positions.

The Briton believes that despite finding more outright pace, McLaren need to build and design a car that is more drivable when pushed to the limit.

"This was a car in which putting together a Qualifying lap was almost impossible, and being as quick as we were was almost impossible," said Norris.

"I mean, I was on pole three times by, I don’t know, two hundredths of a second or something — or not even on pole. So, you know, it wasn’t like we were just winning everything and it was easy.

"The car was probably one of the hardest cars I’ve ever had to drive. But I was putting things together, driving well, and I could get away with it.

"But this isn’t a car you can win a championship with. I still believe a win is possible this year. We just need a quicker car now if we want to get another win.

"But going into next year, we need a car that’s a lot more drivable and easier to drive. Because, yeah, you cannot win a championship with how difficult the car is to drive at the minute."

If he succeeds, the 20-year-old will become the sport’s youngest-ever World Champion but he knows it’s a bit of a long shot to wrap it up this weekend in Austin, Texas.

title: Russell on how 2026 has ‘tested my character and resilience’
excerpt:
George Russell has explained how he approached a series of setbacks that “tested my character and resilience” this season, with the Briton conceding that “it’s a matter of when, not if” Kimi Antonelli seals the Drivers’ Championship.

After a superb start to the year, Russell fell behind his Mercedes team mate and watched as Antonelli’s lead gradually increased as an incompatibility with the car and reliability issues affected his own results.

Victories in Austria and Azerbaijan proved his progress, but with other teams overhauling their respective deficits to Mercedes through upgrades, his chance of winning a maiden title has largely slipped out of his hands.

Antonelli’s first opportunity of being crowned champion comes at this weekend’s United States Grand Prix and partly relies on Russell finishing ninth or lower, but the Briton was prepared to admit that he’s “not in the fight”.

“Whether it’s this weekend or next weekend, it’s a matter of when, not if, he clinches it,” he said. “That’s the reality of the fact. For me, it’s been a very unique season.

“I’ve had to look at myself in the mirror numerous times and think, ‘How do I want to bounce back from these blows?’. Do I just want to give up and accept the misfortune or the poor performances, or do I want to try to rectify things, make the most of it and control everything I can control?

“I can at least be proud of myself that I’ve always put up a fight and always done my utmost to keep myself in the fight. I’ve got a great team around me, and this won’t be my last shot when I’ve got a car beneath me that can fight for victory.

“At the end of this weekend, we’ll see what we can do. We’ll try to get Mercedes back on top because it’s been a while, and let’s see what the future holds.”

Russell and Antonelli are both set to continue racing for the Silver Arrows in 2027, giving the Briton confidence that he can learn from the challenges of this season and come back even stronger in the future.

Russell explained: “I wouldn’t necessarily say there’s a lesson as such, but there have been a lot of things I’ve adapted to and improved on through the struggles I’ve had. It’s been a season that has very much tested my character and resilience.

“I guess I’ve learned a lot about myself being in these moments, because I’ve never really found myself in this position in my career before. So I guess I can say those are the lessons I’ll take forward, and they’ll help me over the next 10 or 15 years of my career.

“I don’t really have any major feelings running through my body when I say that we’re no longer in the fight this season, because when I look back earlier in the year, the things that were keeping me up at night weren’t necessarily about the championship.

“It was more that my performance wasn’t where I wanted it to be. It was like, ‘Well, how am I going to get my performance back to the levels I know I’m capable of? What is it I need from the car? What do I need to change in my driving to get back on top of things?’

“And then, obviously, the misfortune just added salt to the wound. But I intend to be here for many, many, many years to come, and you can’t give up when you’re being kicked to the floor. You’ve got to bounce back. I can at least be proud that I’ve given it my all in that regard.”

title: Verstappen backs Mekies' Red Bull contract extension
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has backed Laurent Mekies' contract extension with Red Bull, but has cautioned those who expect the Dutchman to continue his winning form at this weekend's United States Grand Prix.

It was announced earlier this month that Mekies will remain as Red Bull's CEO and Team Principal until 2031, having joined from Racing Bulls in 2025.

After a slow start under the new-for-2026 regulations, which included building their own engines alongside Ford, Red Bull have shown signs of progress under Mekies' leadership, prompting the new deal.

"It's been great news I think for everyone," said Verstappen during Thursday's media day in Austin on Mekies' contract extension.

"He fully deserves it as well, he's a very hard worker and I think at times this year of course it has not been easy for him as well, but he's a good leader and I think also the atmosphere in the team is great, so it's only right to extend the contract."

Verstappen has claimed dominant victories in the previous two Grands Prix as Red Bull have become the in-form team during the 2026 campaign.

Despite the winning combination, Verstappen is cautious whether he will be able to secure a hat-trick of victories this weekend at COTA, with the venue different to those in Malaysia and Singapore.

"We had two really good weekends, which of course we're very happy with but that is no guarantee that the coming races are going to be like that as well," said Verstappen.

"We had two very hot and humid races and it seemed like also our engine was performing well in these kinds of conditions and now we go of course to a very dry race.

"There are a lot of factors that are a bit different but we'll see. We'll just take it step by step, we don't dream too much, we just stay in the current [frame of mind] and we also know that we want to improve a lot on the car that we can't fix or change for this year, but hopefully for next year."

title: Leclerc names bigger goal than P2 in Teams’ Championship
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has confessed that he doesn’t “really care” about holding onto second place in the Teams’ Championship, with the Monegasque identifying a different goal for Ferrari to reach.

The Scuderia currently sit a comfortable 105 points ahead of McLaren, but as Red Bull have rapidly closed in on the top three, there is still a chance that the battle for P2 could last until the end of the season.

Leclerc believes that instead of prioritising the standings, they should focus their efforts on returning to victory – something they haven’t achieved since he won the British Grand Prix back in July.

Asked how important it is for Ferrari to stay second, he said: “Honestly, the most important thing for us is to focus race by race and try to get as many wins as possible from now until the end of the season, which eventually, as a result, will give us second place in the Constructors’ Championship.

“But second place in the Constructors’ Championship isn’t something I really care about. It’s obviously better than third, but it wouldn’t be a huge satisfaction.

“A much bigger satisfaction would be for us to be able to fight for wins and actually win races before the end of the year. That would also be a good sign to start next year on a high.”

Ferrari have been in contention for the top spot in recent rounds, having clinched a double podium in the Singapore Sprint before Leclerc’s challenge of Max Verstappen faded during the Grand Prix.

Their pace led Isack Hadjar to declare that they were the fastest team at Marina Bay, which Leclerc was quick to reject when speaking ahead of the United States Grand Prix.

“I don’t agree, but to each their own opinion,” he explained. “And, yeah, at the end of the day, we’ll never know, so I think maybe it’s a bit of a pointless discussion.

“But we were happy with our performance in Singapore, although we still have some steps to take. As we’ve seen, Red Bull have taken a step up over the last few races, and they’re enjoying very good momentum. It’s up to us to try to reverse that trend and get back in front.

“I’m pretty sure Mercedes will also, at some point, figure out their new upgrades and get back to where they were before, as will McLaren, which I’ve heard is bringing a significant package here.

“But it’s exciting. I think we’re all relatively close, and it all comes down to small details. We’ve got to be the team that comes out on top.”

title: Ocon: Camara deserves a shot – but I don't deserve to be out
excerpt:
Following last week’s confirmation that Rafael Camara will race for Haas in 2027, the team’s current drivers head into the United States Grand Prix with very different perspectives on the Brazilian’s arrival – although both believe he deserves his opportunity.

Esteban Ocon has known for some time that he will not be driving for Haas next season, with his focus now on securing a seat elsewhere.

Ocon remains confident that he has a future in F1, and a suggestion in Austin on Thursday that he could be making his final appearance at the venue prompted a clear response.

“Don't say that,” Ocon replied. “I'm coming here to do the best job I can, try and exploit the maximum amount of the car. As I said, I deserve to be here in F1.

“There are many circumstances why I'm not here next year, but they are not the performance reasons. I've won everything, in every category I've done – in go-karts, in Formula Renault, in F3, in GP3, in F1.

“In all these categories, I've won races. So, just thinking of a sports perspective, I deserve to be in F1. And yeah, I believe that this is not my last year.”

Asked whether those circumstances related to Haas opting for a Ferrari junior driver, the Frenchman added: “I can't say very much. What I will say is that Rafa deserves a shot in F1. I think he's shown in the [junior] categories that he's very good. But I don't deserve to be out of F1 at the same time. So that's it.”

Knowing that he's looking for a seat, Ocon would not be drawn on which other drivers he felt should make way on the 2027 grid.

“I'm not here to say who deserves [to go and] who doesn't,” the Frenchman said. “But just looking at the results, as I said, Rafa deserves a shot in F1 for sure.

“But I don't deserve to be out in the way that I've had at the moment. Of course, as I said I'm working on a solution for next year, and that's the main target to do well this weekend, and to do well in the next three.”

While Ollie Bearman has yet to be formally confirmed by Haas for 2027, Camara’s arrival presents a very different prospect for the Briton, with the pair having known each other for several years.

“It's funny because we joined Ferrari on the same day,” said Bearman. “We both signed at the same time, and I think we're like three or four days apart in in birthdays. So we can have a joint birthday party next year!

“But no, it's really cool. I think for him, he's been having a really good time in the junior formulas, and I think Haas is a great place to start your F1 career. It's a great team, welcoming, and probably quite different compared to other teams.

“I don't know how some of the other teams are where rookies tend to go, but I've really enjoyed the atmosphere here, and how passionate everybody is as well.”

Exclusive: 'We see huge potential' – Komatsu on choosing Camara for Haas

Bearman will have significantly more F1 experience than Camara when the Brazilian arrives, giving him an opportunity to establish himself as a team leader.

“To be honest, I think I've shown that already,” the Briton added. “I think this year has been a big step for myself in terms of okay on track performance, but more importantly, how I deal with the team, how I transition into that role of leading the team. And I think I've seen a big step in how I deal with the team, but also how the team values my input and my feedback.

“It's definitely important to be cemented as the team leader by having more experience. It's not that I'm not already kind of working well towards that. I think this year has been a big step in that regard, and it's normal coming from F2 that it's not an instant transition, and takes time. But I would say that I've really come a long way in that regard.”

Their shared Ferrari links also mean comparisons between Bearman and Camara are likely to intensify in 2027, with both harbouring ambitions of eventually racing for the Scuderia.

“Of course,” said Bearman. “We're the same age. Obviously, Rafa has less experience than me in F1, but yeah, I guess that for Ferrari it's also a good thing to see who they want to put in their car in the medium term, and of course, my goal is to put myself in the best position for that to be me.”

Bearman may have the upper hand in terms of experience, but the opportunity is clearly there for Camara to ultimately get the nod. After all, Ferrari promoted Charles Leclerc to the works team after a single season at Sauber.

“It's all a question of timing, right?,” said Bearman. “Charles was there for one year. He had a very good year in Sauber that gave him that opportunity.

“In my case, things didn't work out like that. It's always a question of how timing looks, and yeah, that's the reality of F1.”

title: Hamilton reflects on Singapore mistakes ahead of US GP
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has reflected on how his strategy error last time out in Singapore cost himself and Ferrari a podium, and that lessons have been learnt ahead of this weekend's United States Grand Prix.

The seven-time World Champion was on course to finish third in the previous race and secure a double podium for Ferrari behind team mate, Charles Leclerc.

But the Briton failed to pit under a Virtual Safety Car for fresh tyres, a decision made by Hamilton, which meant he ultimately slipped down to sixth at the chequered flag.

During Thursday's media day in Austin, Hamilton was asked to reflect on the decision having claimed that an alternative tyre strategy from the outset was his best chance of beating eventual race winner, Max Verstappen.

"I'm always looking at ways to win. I'm always looking at doing potentially something different and I wanted to be on different strategy to Charles, not where we just follow each other," said Hamilton.

"We assumed Max would be potentially quicker and the strategy [simulation] showed us finishing P2 and P3. That's not enough for me, I wanted to have options.

He added: "In a split second decision I decided to stay out [during the VSC]. As soon as I was alongside the pit lane I knew it was probably the wrong decision but owned up to it, took responsibility for it and you move on.

"We've had good conversations in the background of how we can do better together, how we can collaborate better, but I think nothing's changed in terms of how well we work together in the background.

"I truly believe my job, rather than to follow suit always, is to continuously challenge the team, myself included. Just constantly challenge the norms and that's ultimately how I've got to where I am, and I will not shy away from that.

"Sometimes it doesn't go well, and that was one of those, but you live to fight another day and we win and we lose as a team, so we carry the weight and the cost together.

"It definitely hurts when I lose points for the team, it's not something I do very often, but I'll double the efforts to make sure that doesn't happen again."

Ferrari enjoyed one of their strongest weekends this season in Singapore in terms of pace, with the Scuderia having gradually fallen away as Mercedes' closest challengers over recent rounds.

Hamilton believes there is no reason to suspect that Ferrari will have closed the deficit any further this weekend, despite a small upgrade.

"I think if you look at the rise and different performances through the year, Mercedes were leading for a second, then McLaren stepped up and now you see Red Bull kind of dominating in the last couple of races," he said.

"I don't really see why that would potentially change but I would imagine it's close between us all. I hope if we can get the car in the right place, hopefully we can be there or thereabouts."

title: FIA detail ambitious plans to lower F1 car weight in rules overhaul
excerpt:
The FIA's single-seater technical director has explained plans to cut F1 car weights by nearly 70kg by the time of the next regulation cycle.

The maximum weight of the 2026 machines is 768kg, with this being a reduction of 30kg from the 798kg dry weight in 2025 at the end of the ground effects era.

By the end of the four-year cycle, the cars had ballooned in weight, in part due to the 18-inch wheel rims and bigger tyres, as well as the increased safety devices now used, including the cockpit protection and halo head protection device.

For the next rules cycle, it is clear that F1 will be returning to V8 engines and drop the turbo hybrids, with FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem hopeful this can happen by 2030 or 2031.

It is hoped through a concerted effort that car weights could drop below 700kg for the next rules cycle.

[Article continues below].

FIA's weight reduction hopes

Explaining the coming work to try to get cars back under 700kg, Tombazis explained where the hoped-for-savings would come from.

"We are looking to reduce turbo pressures significantly," Tombazis told The Race.

"That will reduce the pressures both inside the engine and the dimensions of the turbocharger.

"We plan to significantly reduce the complexity of both the inlet and the outlet of the engines - as currently they have a very complex 'spaghetti' of ducts leading into the engine.

"The exhausts are also all tuned for length and so on, so we plan to shorten and simplify those areas a lot."

With the heavy battery systems being dropped for the V8 engines as opposed to the V6 turbo hybrids, further weight savings are planned from this, with a reduction in wheel rim size also anticipated to bring sizeable savings.

Finally, it is hoped that cars will not be required to use as heavy aerodynamic parts when they are lighter and smaller, with this bringing a virtuous circle in terms of weight saving.

"When we do the shopping list and add everything up, we can get quite comfortably below 700kg," Tombazis added.

"Now we are conscious that when we discuss things, there will be some kickback in some areas. We'll have to compromise a bit.

"There will be concerns about certain costs, but overall our target is to be below 700kg, and I think it will be a significant step to make the cars more exciting."

Refuelling will not be reintroduced for the first time since 2009, owing to the added expense, complexity, and dangers of it, and the fact that it limits opportunities for strategic variance.

title: Lando Norris required to 'take tablets' to combat US Grand Prix health concern
excerpt:
Lando Norris has explained how he is required to take "headache tablets" to combat the effects of bumps at the United States Grand Prix venue, Austin.

The Circuit of the Americas was built for the 2012 race on former marshland near Austin Bergstrom International Airport, meaning the ground underneath the track is constantly being forced up and down, with the Texas climate also affecting the track surface.

It was not a concern prior to 2022, with the cars not being run as close to the ground as during the ground effects era of 2022-2025, where downforce was generated by running the car as close to the track surface as possible - thus amplifying the effect of the bumps.

On Thursday ahead of this year's race, Max Verstappen claimed that the bumps situation was "unacceptable" and spoke of the potential for severe spinal damage, having endured peak stresses of 9G at times in the 2025 race.

And Norris believes his fellow world champion Verstappen is "certainly right" with the criticism levied at the track surface.

"I would say yes," Norris told media, including RacingNews365, when presented with Verstappen's "unacceptable" comments.

"If you build a new track now, the FIA has the rules and regulations for building a new track and the tolerances you have to be within are pretty small.

"It certainly doesn't fit anywhere close to what the regulations are now, let's say, but it is an old track, not a new track.

"It is pretty bad, and there are places where I need to take headache tablets before I go out, simply because it is so bumpy and you are hitting your head against the headrests because of the bumps.

"So it is certainly not a nice thing, but there is not a lot we can do.

"We complain about it, and it is brought up many times, but there is only so much we can complain about things, but [Verstappen] is certainly right."

title: George Russell hints at F1 title fight acceptance as 'reality' picture painted
excerpt:
George Russell has stated that his season wasn't "meant to be" as he sits on the verge of a title defeat to team-mate Kimi Antonelli.

Antonelli enters the United States Grand Prix 102 points clear of Russell in the drivers' standings and has his first opportunity to seal the title on Sunday at the Circuit of the Americas.

Russell has faced several hurdles throughout the year, including some reliability woes that have cost him valuable points.

However, the Briton has admitted that in the early stages of the season, his performances were not up to scratch in the fight against Antonelli.

"In terms of my mentality this season, my view of the championship has been up and down," Russell told media including RacingNews365.

"Early in the year when I had a big point deficit, the thing that was keeping me up at night was my lack of performance and thinking, 'how am I going to improve my performance? What do I need from a car?

"'What does the car need from my driving, rather than my opportunity maybe going amiss?'"

[Article continues below]

Russell concedes to 'reality' of difficult F1 season

Russell managed to close the gap at the midpoint of the season when Antonelli had issues of his own, before the gap ballooned up once again in favour of the Italian.

While Russell acknowledged he has had his share of poor luck, the 28-year-old stated his own performances have not been up to standard in comparison to his team-mate.

"I came from 70 points down to within 25 points post-Silverstone, and then the gap extended," he said.

"Baku happened, that felt pretty big in terms of my chances again, and then of course, one week later, you [get] kicked down again, and salt added to the wound with the grid penalty in Singapore.

"This season just hasn't meant to be. I'm not bitter about it.

"I'll look back on the areas I could have done better and should have done better, as opposed to things that have been out of my control that have gone against me.

"As much [that] has gone against me in terms of bad luck, there's been as much of my performances that haven't been to the scratch that I know I'm capable of.

"That's the reality of it."

title: Charles Leclerc hammers Isack Hadjar with 'nonsense' Max Verstappen response
excerpt:
A swift response from Charles Leclerc to an outrageous claim from Isack Hadjar.

Charles Leclerc has dismissed Isack Hadjar's claim that Max Verstappen would have won the Singapore Grand Prix by a bigger margin had he been driving a Ferrari, branding the suggestion "nonsense".

Hadjar made the remark ahead of this weekend's United States Grand Prix, downplaying Red Bull's pace advantage and insisting the Milton Keynes-based team did not have the fastest car on the grid in Singapore, despite Verstappen converting pole into victory.

The Dutchman controlled the race from the front at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, managing his tyres to beat Leclerc by 7.335 seconds, with Kimi Antonelli completing the podium for Mercedes.

Leclerc could not get near the four-time F1 champion in the race, and he was left far from impressed when asked about Hadjar's comments.

Speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, ahead of the Circuit of the Americas weekend, Leclerc made clear he felt Hadjar was in no position to judge.

"I think it's nonsense to start saying these kinds of things," said Leclerc.

"I mean, Isack has no idea what kind of car we drive, and I have no idea what kind of car he drives."

[Article continues below]

Leclerc predicts 'very tight' fight

The Ferrari driver finished second in Singapore after struggling to make progress in Verstappen's dirty air, with team-mate Lewis Hamilton fading to sixth after an extended stint on soft tyres that left him exposed in the closing laps.

Looking ahead to Austin, Leclerc was cautious about predicting how the order might shake out, pointing to how tight the field has become across the back end of the season.

"It's such a tight field that it's very, very difficult for us to predict," he said.

"Yes, of course, we kind of have an idea of how we will be on this track, but when you are speaking about such fine margins, it relies really on optimising your package, and that has a much bigger influence than what we expect in terms of the cars.

"The only outlier in the last few races is that maybe we expected Mercedes to be further ahead than they actually were.

"If they manage to finally unlock the performance that we kind of had in mind for them in the last few races, then I think they will be further ahead than any others, but otherwise, it's going to be very tight."

title: Max Verstappen addresses prospect at being forced to take unwanted F1 penalty
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has not ruled out the prospect of being forced to take an engine penalty in the remainder of the 2026 F1 season.

The Red Bull driver has thus far not taken a engine grid penalty in the campaign, and is on the final penalty-free example of the Internal Combustion Engine, turbocharger, MGU-K, energy store, control electronics, and the exhaust systems.

He has also used five of the six permitted power unit ancillary components, meaning he would have to get to seven used before a penalty is incurred.

In contrast, team-mate Isack Hadjar took a five-place grid drop in Malaysia for a new ICE, and took a pit-lane start in Singapore for a new ICE, turbocharger, exhaust, and PU-ANC.

In Italy, Liam Lawson took a full whack penalty of every component and was sent to the back of the field, although this counted towards the total of Hadjar's car with Lawson deputising for the injured Frenchman at the time.

Verstappen has also suffered two power unit related retirements in 2026, with a coolant leak forcing him out in China, before an engine failure off the line in Monaco ended his race on Lap 1.

When asked if a potential penalty was incoming over the final six rounds of the season, Verstappen, who has won the previous two races in Sepang and Singapore, did not rule it out.

"That we have to take a penalty at one point, yeah, potentially," Verstappen told media, including RacingNews365.

"But there's no known date to that at the moment.

"So we just see what happens."

title: Oliver Bearman issues firm declaration over F1 future amid new contract delay
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman believes he "is ready" to move to a "top four team" in F1 and be able to fight "for podiums" as his new contract at Haas is delayed.

That Bearman will remain at Haas for a third season in 2027 is not in doubt, with team boss Ayao Komatsu playing up his strengths as the new team leader, with fellow Ferrari junior Rafael Camara set to replace Esteban Ocon.

Bearman is the most senior driver within the Ferrari Driver Academy and is the first in line for a promotion to the senior works Ferrari squad, should a seat become available, but with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in his way, it is unclear when this would open up.

Hamilton has also indicated that he could be on the grid for F1's return to Africa, sometime in the early 2030s.

Bearman's seat at Haas for 2027 is just one of three seats yet to be officially confirmed, with the two Racing Bulls cockpits also vacant for next season, with the Briton declaring that "only sticking points" remained before his stay at Haas was extended - as he also made clear that he is ready for a move to a "top four" team.

"On my side and on Ayao's side, I think we're very sure that we want to continue working together, and the only sticking points are out of my hands," Bearman explained to media, including RacingNews365.

"They are more contractual points, but it is out of my hands. I am leaving it to my management, and of course, Ferrari as well.

"I'm committed to Haas, and the length of the deal is not really my remit.

"I'm happy to be in F1, but of course, looking into the medium- to long-term, I also feel like I am ready to fight for podiums and fight at the front.

"In terms of a midfield team, Haas is the team I want to be with and see my future with, but at some point, I feel like I've earned the opportunity to go out and look for a top four team.

"Of course, my link with Ferrari will be my ultimate goal, but I'm not discussing the nitty-gritty [of the Haas renewal].

"That's what my short-term ambition is, and my medium- to long-term [goal] is of course, to be fighting for podiums.

"I hope Haas can give me that opportunity, but of course, Ferrari are involved."

[Article continues below].

Bearman's Ferrari links

Bearman has already driven for Ferrari in a grand prix, doing so in Saudi Arabia in 2024 in place of an appendicitis-stricken Carlos Sainz, finishing seventh ahead of Lando Norris and Hamilton.

This result was a key pillar in Ferrari's decision to promote him to F1 full-time in 2025 with Haas, as he explained that the Scuderia will continue to have a "big say" in his future.

"In the end, I am a junior driver of Ferrari, and that's ultimately the reason I'm here," he added.

"So they have a big say in what my future looks like."

title: Kimi Antonelli wary 'catastrophe' needed to realise 'crazy' childhood dream
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has admitted it would take a "catastrophic" collapse from his title rivals for him to be crowned F1 world champion this weekend, as the Mercedes driver arrives in Austin holding a commanding 102-point lead over George Russell.

Antonelli tops the drivers' standings on 340 points after eight wins in 2026, with Russell second on 238 ahead of Lewis Hamilton (229), Max Verstappen (221), Charles Leclerc (215) and Lando Norris (201).

The United States Grand Prix runs as a standard weekend with no sprint, meaning a maximum of 25 points is on offer at the Circuit of the Americas. That makes it mathematically impossible for the title to be wrapped up before Sunday's chequered flag.

For Antonelli to clinch the championship in Austin on Sunday, he would need to win the race while his closest challenger, Russell, finishes no higher than ninth and Hamilton no higher than fourth.

Should he seal it this weekend, Antonelli, who turned 20 in August, would become the youngest world champion in F1 history, beating the record of 23 years and 134 days set by Sebastian Vettel in 2010.

Speaking to select media including RacingNews365 ahead of the weekend, Antonelli played down the prospect.

"I mean, definitely it's crazy if you think about it, but that's why I won't think about it," he said.

"Something catastrophic needs to happen to others for me to become [world champion]. For me, it needs to be a perfect weekend, and to the others, they need to do poor results, which is unlikely to happen. So, of course, anything can happen, and it's crazy to think about it."

"But as I said, we had a meeting with Bono this morning, and we just said, just have fun, just always the same mindset as I had all year, one race at a time, and yeah, just try to do the best I can every race weekend, and then we'll see. But of course, if I do things well, then the result will come."

Kimi Antonelli fully aware F1 title fight 'not over yet'

Antonelli's 2026 campaign has been a mesmeric one, particularly given how dramatically his rookie year collapsed during the European races.

Asked what it would mean to lift the title at just 20 years old, Antonelli did not hide his emotion, while insisting the job is far from done.

"It will be a dream," he said. "It's something I dreamt of since I was little. First of all, really to find myself in such a position is is incredible. But at the same time, I need to keep going, keep pushing, and it's not over yet."

"So first, we'll try to finish the job properly, and then yeah, we can enjoy the rest [of the season]. But for sure, it will be an incredible achievement. But still there's a bit to go."

title: Isack Hadjar counters Red Bull position : 'If Max had driven the Ferrari...'
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar believes Max Verstappen could have won the Singapore Grand Prix in a Ferrari, suggesting Red Bull's RB22 was not the fastest car on the grid despite his team-mate's victory.

Verstappen took the win in Singapore after qualifying on pole, beating Charles Leclerc's Ferrari by 7.335 seconds, with Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli in third.

Hadjar, by contrast, endured a miserable weekend, retiring from the sprint with a PU failure before a replacement engine shut down again and triggered a total gearbox failure in qualifying, leaving him without a representative lap time and down in 22nd on the grid. He eventually finished 10th in the race.

Speaking to media in Austin ahead of the United States Grand Prix, Hadjar reflected on a frustrating run of reliability issues before turning to the pace of the car itself.

"It was one of those weekends where you get a failure in each session, so you learn from it, and we just move on," said Hadjar.

"I'm happy to be here in Texas. I like the track, and, performance-wise, the car has been working really well the last couple of weekends.

"We're confident as a team, but, of course, we're aware of the upgrades on the cars in the other garages, so we're still down to earth.

"We still know our weaknesses on the car. We're still working on it, so I just want to go out there and have another clean one because the last two weekends have been very frustrating considering the car I've been given."

[Article continues below]

Hadjar - 'Hard to drive'

Asked directly whether Red Bull has arrived in Texas with the fastest car, Hadjar was blunt. "No, I don't think we have the fastest car," he replied.

Pressed on why, the French-Algerian driver pointed to the RB22's handling rather than raw straight-line or downforce numbers, pointing to Verstappen and what he could have achieved if he had been behind the wheel of Ferrari's SF-26.

"Because I think the car is still very hard to drive," he said.

"In Malaysia, it was dominant, but I don't think in Singapore it was the fastest car. That's what I believe.

"I think if you'd put Max in the Ferrari, he would have won the race with more margin. That's my opinion. In Singapore, I think it was the fastest car."

title: F1 and FIA warned over 'relatively premature' Middle East decision
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz feels it is "relatively premature" for F1 and the FIA to sound so convinced that the season-ending grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead as planned.

Both governing bodies have repeatedly stated in recent weeks that the Gulf events remain on track, even as regional tensions linked to the conflict involving Iran have prompted scrutiny of travel routes and personnel safety across the area.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has maintained that the organisation works directly with promoters and governments in the region and will not send competitors or staff anywhere it deems unsafe, while insisting current conditions support going ahead with both races.

F1 chief executive Stefano Domenicali's organisation, meanwhile, has continued reviewing security assessments alongside the relevant authorities.

Williams driver Sainz, though, has warned that the geopolitical situation in the Middle East could still shift dramatically before the cars reach Lusail.

Sainz has questioned the certainty being projected by the sport's leadership given how much could still change in the coming weeks.

"They seem very convinced that they're going to go ahead," said Grand Prix Drivers' Association director Sainz, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, ahead of this weekend's United States Grand Prix in Austin, Texas.

"On my personal side, and not speaking as the GPDA, it's very difficult to be convinced right now because there are still plenty of things happening in the Middle East.

"Also, there is obviously an election that is going to happen in the U.S. [referring to the midterms] and things that are going to happen on the political side of the world that could affect the next month, month and a half, very suddenly.

"I think it's relatively premature to be so convinced."

[Article continues below]

Sainz - 'We need to follow their lead'

Sainz, however, stopped short of calling for the races to be scrapped, stressing that drivers are reliant on information they simply do not have access to.

"As it stands, we would go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, and if the FIA and Formula 1 decide that it's still safe and a good scenario, I think we, as drivers, have to go with whatever they say," said the Spaniard.

"We don't have as much political information, as much inside information as they have, so we need to follow their lead and trust in their decision-making.

"But as it stands, the world can change a lot in the next month, month and a half, and we need to stay diligent and reactive to whatever happens, and not just go because we want to go right now."

It is understood that if the two races are cancelled at any stage, then F1 would head to the Italian circuit of Imola for the season-ending grand prix over the first weekend in December.

title: Lando Norris and George Russell offer clarity over Red Bull simulator outings
excerpt:
Lando Norris and George Russell have shed light on comments made by Christian Horner regarding their use of Red Bull's simulator in the past.

Horner recently stated that Norris and Russell, as well as Oscar Piastri, “were paying us [Red Bull] to go on our simulator“, during his time as the Milton Keynes-based squad's team principal.

Both Norris and Russell were asked about the remark ahead of the United States Grand Prix weekend.

Reigning champion Norris insisted it was several years before he joined the McLaren programme, and was simply a chance to gain knowledge as he started his single-seater career.

“This is when I was like 13, this was way before McLaren,” Norris told media including RacingNews365. “I couldn't be driving someone else's sim when I'm with McLaren.

“This was when I was like five years, four years before McLaren. I've not seen any of this or heard any of it.

“I was doing it with a lot of different teams. I was trying to get experience. I was learning from different people.

“At that age, it's more valuable than ever to do as much as you possibly can.

“I drove on different simulators from different teams because it was a good thing for me, especially at that age.

“I don't know what came out of it after that. So it was more just for my own learning than anything else.”

[Article continues below]

Russell reveals Formula Renault experience on Red Bull simulator

Russell told a similar story, stating he used the simulator to prepare for Formula Renault in 2014.

“Back in 2013, simulators weren't really a thing for anybody,” Russell stated.

“Junior teams didn't have simulators. There was an opportunity to do some driving on that simulator in the Formula Renault car.

“So it was more as preparation for testing and driving for the series that we were racing.

“No teams had it, so that's the extent of it.”

title: Charles Leclerc airs 'notebook' revelation on Lewis Hamilton: 'More than ever'
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has revealed he is filling notebooks with observations on Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton at a rate he has never experienced before.

The contrasting styles between Leclerc and Hamilton have been well documented, with the seven-time F1 champion favouring late, straight-line braking and a stable rear end, while the Monégasque leans on heavy trail braking and a more rotational approach through corner entry.

Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur has previously stated those differing preferences have, if anything, widened the scope of the team's development work rather than created a problem to be solved.

That technical gap has not stopped Leclerc from studying his team-mate closely. Asked whether the pair had pushed each other to become better drivers this season, Leclerc did not hesitate.

"100 per cent," he said. "To push each other every weekend, there are some weekends where he's just incredibly quick, and I learn a huge amount.

"And when I'm doing a good job, I still learn a huge amount from Lewis in just looking at the data and trying to understand the way he works and the way he just deals with the car because he's incredibly good at it.

"There's always something to take after each weekend. I've got my notebook with a lot of notes, and probably more notes than ever since Lewis joined the team."

[Article continues below]

Leclerc on Ferrari upgrade expectations

Leclerc's remarks came as Ferrari prepares to roll out a fourth and final major aerodynamic update for the SF-26 for this weekend's United States Grand Prix, featuring a revised floor aimed at cutting drag. But the 29-year-old was careful not to oversell it.

"They're not that major," Leclerc said of the upgrades. "I've heard quite a lot about them, but they are not as big as maybe what's going around. It's a small step in the right direction, obviously. As always, that's the target.

"Then we still need to put it on the car and do the first three laps and see whether the step we expected is there.

"However, I've heard other teams are bringing big upgrades, so we'll have to see how it compares to them, but I don't expect anything hugely significant.

"I hope it can help us just make that little step forward and win the race as well."

title: Max Verstappen reveals extent of spine damage after years of racing
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has disclosed the physical toll of his years spent racing, revealing that medical checks have shown damage to the lower end of his spine.

Speaking in Austin ahead of the United States Grand Prix, the four-time F1 champion detailed the vertical forces drivers are subjected to during a race weekend, singling out the bumpy Circuit of the Americas as a particularly brutal example.

Verstappen said the loads involved go well beyond the cornering forces drivers are usually associated with.

When going into detail on the spinal impact in Austin, Verstappen explained: "So last year, for example, you pull around 5–6G in a corner.

"But I had some impacts, like vertical loads, which were over 9G on my spine, which I can tell you is really not fun.

"And especially the older you get, you think about that more and more. That's not what you want.

"With these cars, especially under braking, you bottom out way harder because when the wings close and the ride height comes down under braking, it's actually a very stressful moment.

"I know around here, in some places, it's very bumpy under braking, and especially when there are these kinds of awkward bumps, not just bumps from the track getting older, but the surface underneath, the soil, just moving up and down, it's sometimes very hard to expect.

"Or if you're a tiny bit offline, you don't know what is there because no one really drives here sometimes. It's really not nice, and I think something people don't really understand.

"I can tell you from the checks I've had on my spine, the bottom end doesn't look that great."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen - 'It's not nice'

The Red Bull driver's comments come after years of complaints from the grid about the physical consequences of the ground-effect era, which was introduced in 2022 and forced teams to run their cars at minimal ride heights with stiff suspension to keep the floor 'sealed' against the track.

That combination was repeatedly flagged as a safety concern, leading to several drivers reporting back problems and the FIA eventually stepping in with technical directives aimed at limiting the vertical bouncing known as porpoising.

Although the ground-effect cars made way for new regulations at the start of this season, Verstappen has made clear he does not see the physical punishment as an unavoidable part of competing at the top level.

"I know that's part of racing," he said. "I know that can be part of sport, but it's also further damage from the cars we've had over the last few years.

"And now, if we continue finding this acceptable to drive on, then you are going to suffer with that much more.

"People can say, 'Yeah, but you know there are worse sports out there where you can damage parts of your body.' For sure, but that's why I'm not doing them. So, yeah, it's not nice."

title: Liam Lawson 'feeling a lot of things' ahead of debut concert at US GP
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has admitted he is "feeling a lot of things" as he prepares to take to the stage at the Circuit of the Americas on Thursday.

The Racing Bulls driver will set up and perform music in front of a crowd in the build-up to the United States Grand Prix this weekend.

Lawson has long shared his passion for music, with clips often shared online of him performing, both recently and when he was growing up.

It will mark the first time in 11 years that Lawson has played in front of a crowd, and he admitted he is feeling nervous about the prospect.

"I am feeling a lot of things," Lawson told media including RacingNews365.

"It's a cool opportunity to do this with my brother and a couple of friends that I've grown up playing with.

"To be honest, we haven't done this for like 10 years.

"We never really performed, but we grew up playing together when we were very young, so it's a cool opportunity.

"But no, I'm shitting myself, for sure.

"I would happily get in an F1 car and go out for Q3 over doing this!"

[Article continues below]

Lawson explains root of passion for music

Lawson has enjoyed a strong F1 campaign so far as he looks to retain his seat at Racing Bulls for the 2027 season.

While he has forged a career out of racing, Lawson has a deep passion for music, which he revealed comes from his father.

"It's from my dad, my dad plays in a band," he said. "He's played his whole life.

"He got me and my brother into it, and some of my earliest memories are watching him play guitar, watching him play with his bands.

"He performed and played it at his own 40th. It was really, really cool. It's something that has been in my family, that's what got me into it."
